papers.title: Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and whether insights from circuit analysis generalize across tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and that interventions based on one circuit can improve performance on another task, providing evidence for task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.conclusion: Circuit components are reused across tasks, providing evidence that large language models' behavior can be explained in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.key_findings:
The IOI circuit reproduces on GPT2-Medium, with minor differences such as the negative mover head attending only to the S2 token.
The Colored Objects circuit shares about 78% of the important attention heads with the IOI circuit, indicating high component reuse.
Interventions on inhibition heads and the negative mover head can boost accuracy on the Colored Objects task from 49.6% to 93.7%.
The inhibition-mover head subcircuit behaves invariantly across tasks, as predicted by the IOI circuit.
The negative mover head in GPT2-Medium exhibits more sophisticated behavior than in GPT2-Small, directly demoting the subject token.
papers.limitation:
Quantifying circuit overlap is complex and not fully addressed in this paper.
The generality of the circuit beyond the studied tasks is not confirmed.
future_direction: Understanding how commonly the mover circuit is used by GPT2 in other tasks.
Developing methods for quantifying circuit overlap.
Studying circuit reuse in larger models.
papers.abstract: Recent work in mechanistic interpretability has shown that behaviors in language models can be successfully reverse-engineered through circuit analysis. A common criticism, however, is that each circuit is task-specific, and thus such analysis cannot contribute to understanding the models at a higher level. In this work, we present evidence that insights (both low-level findings about specific heads and higher-level findings about general algorithms) can indeed generalize across tasks. Specifically, we study the circuit discovered in Wang et al. (2022) for the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task and 1.) show that it reproduces on a larger GPT2 model, and 2.) that it is mostly reused to solve a seemingly different task: Colored Objects (Ippolito & Callison-Burch, 2023). We provide evidence that the process underlying both tasks is functionally very similar, and contains about a 78% overlap in in-circuit attention heads. We further present a proof-of-concept intervention experiment, in which we adjust four attention heads in middle layers in order to 'repair' the Colored Objects circuit and make it behave like the IOI circuit. In doing so, we boost accuracy from 49.6% to 93.7% on the Colored Objects task and explain most sources of error. The intervention affects downstream attention heads in specific ways predicted by their interactions in the IOI circuit, indicating that this subcircuit behavior is invariant to the different task inputs. Overall, our results provide evidence that it may yet be possible to explain large language models' behavior in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks and computational components.

papers.title: Opening the Black Box: A Survey on the Mechanisms of Multi-Step Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that enable multi-step reasoning in large language models, covering both implicit (latent) and explicit (e.g., Chain-of-Thought) reasoning paradigms?
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying multi-step reasoning in large language models, organizing existing research around seven interconnected research questions and highlighting future research directions.
papers.conclusion: The survey concludes by highlighting five open research directions for future mechanistic understanding of multi-step reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Implicit multi-hop reasoning in LLMs is an orchestrated, layered process with distinct modules specializing in different phases, but it is constrained by the fixed depth of transformers.
Implicit reasoning capability emerges via grokking, a phase transition from memorization to generalization, influenced by training data distribution, data scale, and optimization biases.
LLMs frequently bypass genuine multi-step reasoning by using shortcuts, such as direct input-output associations (factual shortcuts) or surface-level heuristics (structural shortcuts).
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting activates a 'reasoning mode' where models use generated tokens as external memory, breaking the depth limitation and enhancing computational expressiveness and generalization.
CoT does not equate to faithful explainability; it often functions as post-hoc rationalization due to a structural mismatch between the distributed, parallel computation of transformers and the sequential nature of explicit reasoning.
future_direction: Rigorous causal analysis in real-world settings
Bridging the faithfulness gap of explicit CoT reasoning
Mechanistic understanding of Latent CoT reasoning
White-box evaluation metrics for LLM reasoning
From mechanistic interpretation to model control
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities to solve problems requiring multiple reasoning steps, yet the internal mechanisms enabling such capabilities remain elusive. Unlike existing surveys that primarily focus on engineering methods to enhance performance, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying LLM multi-step reasoning. We organize the survey around a conceptual framework comprising seven interconnected research questions, from how LLMs execute implicit multi-hop reasoning within hidden activations to how verbalized explicit reasoning remodels the internal computation. Finally, we highlight five research directions for future mechanistic studies.

papers.title: NeuroFaith: Evaluating LLM Self-Explanation Faithfulness via Internal Representation Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we measure the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations by aligning them with the model's internal reasoning processes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeuroFaith, a framework that measures faithfulness of LLM self-explanations by extracting concepts from explanations and mechanistically testing their influence on predictions, and shows how to detect and improve faithfulness via linear probing and steering.
papers.conclusion: NeuroFaith provides a principled approach to evaluating and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations, addressing critical needs for trustworthy AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models tend to produce more faithful and correct self-explanations.
Models can arrive at correct answers through alternative reasoning pathways that bypass explicit bridge object computation (shortcut learning).
There is a gap between internal reasoning and expressed explanations, which decreases with model size.
NeuroFaith outperforms existing faithfulness measures (Counterfactual Intervention and Attribution Agreement) in several settings.
Faithfulness can be linearly detected in representation space and improved through steering.
papers.limitation: Human annotation for concept extraction is costly and may not scale, while LLM-as-a-Judge approaches offer scalability but may miss relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate plausible free text self-explanations to justify their answers. However, these natural language explanations may not accurately reflect the model's actual reasoning process, pinpointing a lack of faithfulness. Existing faithfulness evaluation methods rely primarily on behavioral tests or computational block analysis without examining the semantic content of internal neural representations. This paper proposes NeuroFaith, a flexible framework that measures the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanation by identifying key concepts within explanations and mechanistically testing whether these concepts actually influence the model's predictions. We show the versatility of NeuroFaith across 2-hop reasoning and classification tasks. Additionally, we develop a linear faithfulness probe based on NeuroFaith to detect unfaithful self-explanations from representation space and improve faithfulness through steering. NeuroFaith provides a principled approach to evaluating and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations, addressing critical needs for trustworthy AI systems.

papers.title: From Yes-Men to Truth-Tellers: Addressing Sycophancy in Large Language Models with Pinpoint Tuning
papers.research_question: How can we address sycophancy in Large Language Models by pinpointing and tuning only the components responsible for this behavior, without degrading their general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes supervised pinpoint tuning (SPT), a method that identifies a sparse set of attention heads responsible for sycophancy using path patching and then fine-tunes only those heads, effectively mitigating sycophancy while preserving the model's general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Pinpoint tuning is an effective and efficient method to address sycophancy in LLMs by targeting specific internal components, advancing both the understanding and intervention of model behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Only a small percentage (~4%) of attention heads significantly influence sycophantic behavior, as identified by path patching.
Pinpoint tuning these heads effectively reduces sycophancy, outperforming supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on sycophancy metrics.
Pinpoint tuning preserves general capabilities (e.g., reasoning, math, code) unlike SFT, which often degrades them.
The method generalizes beyond the training data, as shown on additional sycophancy evaluation datasets.
The identified sycophancy-related heads attend more to tokens that challenge the model compared to other heads.
papers.limitation:
Path patching treats each MLP and attention head as individual nodes, but future work could consider neurons or groups of neurons as atomic units for more refined analysis.
The evaluation is based on a specific definition of sycophancy (from Sharma et al. 2023), and it is unclear whether the results generalize to other formats of sycophancy.
The verification of pinpoint tuning is mainly conducted on sycophancy; its effectiveness for other abilities requires further investigation.
future_direction: Treating neurons or groups of neurons as atomic units for analysis instead of heads and MLPs.
Investigating generalization to other formats and definitions of sycophancy.
Integrating pinpoint tuning with other interpretability tools like information flow, representation engineering, and sparse auto-encoders.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) tend to prioritize adherence to user prompts over providing veracious responses, leading to the sycophancy issue. When challenged by users, LLMs tend to admit mistakes and provide inaccurate responses even if they initially provided the correct answer. Recent works propose to employ supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to mitigate the sycophancy issue, while it typically leads to the degeneration of LLMs' general capability. To address the challenge, we propose a novel supervised pinpoint tuning (SPT), where the region-of-interest modules are tuned for a given objective. Specifically, SPT first reveals and verifies a small percentage (<5%) of the basic modules, which significantly affect a particular behavior of LLMs. i.e., sycophancy. Subsequently, SPT merely fine-tunes these identified modules while freezing the rest. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed SPT, we conduct comprehensive experiments, demonstrating that SPT significantly mitigates the sycophancy issue of LLMs (even better than SFT). Moreover, SPT introduces limited or even no side effects on the general capability of LLMs. Our results shed light on how to precisely, effectively, and efficiently explain and improve the targeted ability of LLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/yellowtownhz/sycophancy-interpretability.

papers.title: Understanding Fact Recall in Language Models: Why Two-Stage Training Encourages Memorization but Mixed Training Teaches Knowledge
papers.research_question: Why does two-stage training encourage memorization while mixed training teaches knowledge, and how do shared parameters internally support fact recall in mixed training?
papers.core_contribution: Mixed training teaches knowledge by increasing the quantity and collective importance of shared parameters, which are concentrated in critical attention heads for fact recall. The paper introduces cross-task gradient trace to analyze these parameters.
papers.conclusion: Mixed training teaches knowledge by increasing the quantity and collective importance of shared parameters, which are concentrated in critical attention heads for fact recall. The cross-task gradient trace tool can be used to analyze such mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Mixed training yields more shared parameters (those influenced by both fact-storing and fact-recalling examples) than two-stage training.
Shared parameters are concentrated in critical attention heads and are key to enabling fact recall in mixed-trained models.
Ablating shared parameters leads to a larger performance drop in mixed-trained models compared to two-stage trained models.
Mixed training achieves more parameter-efficient fact recall, requiring fewer parameters to recover performance.
Shared parameters in mixed training are more centralized and functionally important for generalization.
future_direction: Explore whether similar mechanisms emerge in other cross-task settings.
papers.abstract: Fact recall, the ability of language models (LMs) to retrieve specific factual knowledge, remains a challenging task despite their impressive general capabilities. Common training strategies often struggle to promote robust recall behavior with two-stage training, which first trains a model with fact-storing examples (e.g., factual statements) and then with fact-recalling examples (question-answer pairs), tending to encourage rote memorization rather than generalizable fact retrieval. In contrast, mixed training, which jointly uses both types of examples, has been empirically shown to improve the ability to recall facts, but the underlying mechanisms are still poorly understood. In this work, we investigate how these training strategies affect how model parameters are shaped during training and how these differences relate to their ability to recall facts. We introduce cross-task gradient trace to identify shared parameters, those strongly influenced by both fact-storing and fact-recalling examples. Our analysis on synthetic fact recall datasets with the Llama-3.2B and Pythia-2.8B models reveals that mixed training encouraging a larger and more centralized set of shared parameters. These findings suggest that the emergence of parameters may play a key role in enabling LMs to generalize factual knowledge across task formulations.

papers.title: Mechanism and Emergence of Stacked Attention Heads in Multi-Layer Transformers
papers.research_question: What tasks require transformers of a specific depth? Can large language models solve such tasks without fine-tuning? What mechanism do transformers use to solve the task? How does this mechanism emerge during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the retrieval problem, a task requiring a minimum number of transformer layers, and uncovers that transformers solve it using stacked attention heads (retrieval heads) which emerge gradually via an implicit curriculum.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces the retrieval problem, shows it requires a certain number of layers, and finds transformers solve it using a mechanism resembling an induction head that emerges gradually with the help of an implicit curriculum.
papers.key_findings:
The retrieval problem requires a minimum number of transformer layers that grows logarithmically with the number of retrieval steps.
Large language models can solve the retrieval problem without any specific fine-tuning.
Transformers solve the retrieval problem using stacked attention heads that resemble induction heads.
Retrieval heads emerge gradually during training, one head at a time, guided by an implicit curriculum.
The implicit curriculum is essential for successful learning of the retrieval problem.
papers.limitation:
The analysis of transformers trained on a minimal formulation of the retrieval problem might not generalize perfectly to large language models.
The paper does not provide a full explanation of the training dynamics of transformers on the retrieval problem.
future_direction: Further research is needed to fully understand the multi-layered circuits learned by large language models and the training dynamics that enable their learning.
papers.abstract: In this paper, I introduce the retrieval problem, a simple yet common reasoning task that can be solved only by transformers with a minimum number of layers, which grows logarithmically with the input size. I empirically show that large language models can solve the task under different prompting formulations without any fine-tuning. To understand how transformers solve the retrieval problem, I train several transformers on a minimal formulation. Successful learning occurs only under the presence of an implicit curriculum. I uncover the learned mechanisms by studying the attention maps in the trained transformers. I also study the training process, uncovering that attention heads always emerge in a specific sequence guided by the implicit curriculum.

papers.title: On the Behavior of Convolutional Nets for Feature Extraction
papers.research_question: How discriminative are individual CNN features for characterizing classes across different datasets, and how can they be used for knowledge representation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a statistical analysis of individual CNN features for feature extraction, showing that features can be discriminative by both their presence and absence, and that convolutional features are more general and discriminant than previously thought, enabling their use for knowledge representation without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: CNN features, especially from convolutional layers, are highly discriminative and can be used for knowledge representation by both presence and absence, with context being key in the feature extraction process.
papers.key_findings:
Features can be characteristic of a class by their presence or their absence, providing two modalities of information.
Convolutional features are more general and discriminant than previously considered, opening their use for knowledge representation and unsupervised learning.
Low and middle level features behave similarly across datasets, indicating they can be used for knowledge representation on a wide variety of datasets without fine-tuning.
The relevance of fully-connected features is strongly tied to the similarity between the source and target tasks; for dissimilar tasks, they behave similarly to convolutional features.
A thresholding method based on statistical distance can be applied to remove noisy features, with the threshold correlated to the number of images per class.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are representation learning techniques. During training, a deep net is capable of generating a descriptive language of unprecedented size and detail in machine learning. Extracting the descriptive language coded within a trained CNN model (in the case of image data), and reusing it for other purposes is a field of interest, as it provides access to the visual descriptors previously learnt by the CNN after processing millions of images, without requiring an expensive training phase. Contributions to this field (commonly known as feature representation transfer or transfer learning) have been purely empirical so far, extracting all CNN features from a single layer close to the output and testing their performance by feeding them to a classifier. This approach has provided consistent results, although its relevance is limited to classification tasks. In a completely different approach, in this paper we statistically measure the discriminative power of every single feature found within a deep CNN, when used for characterizing every class of 11 datasets. We seek to provide new insights into the behavior of CNN features, particularly the ones from convolutional layers, as this can be relevant for their application to knowledge representation and reasoning. Our results confirm that low and middle level features may behave differently to high level features, but only under certain conditions. We find that all CNN features can be used for knowledge representation purposes both by their presence or by their absence, doubling the information a single CNN feature may provide. We also study how much noise these features may include, and propose a thresholding approach to discard most of it. All these insights have a direct application to the generation of CNN embedding spaces.

papers.title: Finding Transformer Circuits with Edge Pruning
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and accurately discover sparse computational subgraphs (circuits) in transformers that capture specific model behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Edge Pruning, an efficient and scalable gradient-based pruning method for automated circuit discovery that finds sparser and more faithful circuits than prior methods.
papers.conclusion: Edge Pruning is a practical and scalable tool for interpretability that can shed light on behaviors emerging in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Edge Pruning finds circuits in GPT-2 that use less than half the edges of prior methods while being equally faithful on standard tasks.
The method scales effectively to 100K examples and to CodeLlama-13B, a model over 100x larger than GPT-2.
It perfectly recovers ground-truth circuits in Tracr-compiled models.
A case study on CodeLlama-13B reveals substantial overlap between circuits for instruction-prompted and in-context learning settings, suggesting shared mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The method's reliance on providing corrupted examples for interchange ablation.
Potential challenges in converging to very high sparsity regimes.
future_direction: Improving the efficiency and scalability of the method further.
Applying Edge Pruning to more complex tasks and model behaviors.
Exploring the method's applicability to other model architectures.
papers.abstract: The path to interpreting a language model often proceeds via analysis of circuits -- sparse computational subgraphs of the model that capture specific aspects of its behavior. Recent work has automated the task of discovering circuits. Yet, these methods have practical limitations, as they rely either on inefficient search algorithms or inaccurate approximations. In this paper, we frame automated circuit discovery as an optimization problem and propose *Edge Pruning* as an effective and scalable solution. Edge Pruning leverages gradient-based pruning techniques, but instead of removing neurons or components, it prunes the \emph{edges} between components. Our method finds circuits in GPT-2 that use less than half the number of edges compared to circuits found by previous methods while being equally faithful to the full model predictions on standard circuit-finding tasks. Edge Pruning is efficient even with as many as 100K examples, outperforming previous methods in speed and producing substantially better circuits. It also perfectly recovers the ground-truth circuits in two models compiled with Tracr. Thanks to its efficiency, we scale Edge Pruning to CodeLlama-13B, a model over 100x the scale that prior methods operate on. We use this setting for a case study comparing the mechanisms behind instruction prompting and in-context learning. We find two circuits with more than 99.96% sparsity that match the performance of the full model and reveal that the mechanisms in the two settings overlap substantially. Our case study shows that Edge Pruning is a practical and scalable tool for interpretability and sheds light on behaviors that only emerge in large models.

papers.title: Large Language Models Are Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between cross-lingual transferability and the components of reasoning tasks (knowledge retrieval vs. knowledge-free reasoning)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that knowledge-free reasoning capability transfers nearly perfectly across languages, whereas knowledge retrieval significantly hinders cross-lingual transfer, attributed to shared neural mechanisms for reasoning and language-specific knowledge storage.
papers.conclusion: The demand for knowledge retrieval significantly hinders cross-lingual transfer performance, while knowledge-free reasoning ability can be nearly fully transferred between languages, due to shared neural mechanisms for reasoning and language-specific knowledge storage.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge retrieval component significantly hinders cross-lingual transfer in reasoning tasks; more knowledge retrieval leads to lower transfer effectiveness.
Knowledge-free reasoning capability can be nearly perfectly transferred across languages after fine-tuning in one language.
Cross-lingual computational similarity (hidden states and neuron activation) is higher for knowledge-free reasoning than for knowledge retrieval, especially in middle layers.
Target language proficiency impacts transferability; improving proficiency enhances cross-lingual transfer for knowledge-free reasoning.
The model uses similar neurons for knowledge-free reasoning across languages, while knowledge is stored separately in different languages.
papers.limitation:
Limited model selection and language coverage, primarily relying on LLaMA-2 and only ten languages.
Depth of interpretability analysis is limited; macro-level numerical analyses without precisely identifying specific neurons.
future_direction: Conduct more detailed neuron-level analyses to verify hypotheses about shared neurons for reasoning and language-specific knowledge storage.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated impressive reasoning capabilities across multiple languages. However, the relationship between capabilities in different languages is less explored. In this work, we decompose the process of reasoning tasks into two separated components: knowledge retrieval and knowledge-free reasoning, and analyze the relationship between cross-lingual transferability and these two components. With adapted commonsense reasoning datasets and constructed knowledge-free reasoning datasets, we show that the knowledge-free reasoning capability can be nearly perfectly transferred across various source-target language directions despite the secondary impact of resource in some specific target languages, while cross-lingual knowledge retrieval significantly hinders the transfer. Moreover, by analyzing the hidden states and feed-forward network neuron activation during the reasoning, we show that higher similarity of hidden representations and larger overlap of activated neurons could explain the better cross-lingual transferability of knowledge-free reasoning than knowledge retrieval. Thus, we hypothesize that knowledge-free reasoning shares similar neurons in different languages for reasoning, while knowledge is stored separately in different languages. Our code and data is available at: https://github.com/NJUNLP/Knowledge-Free-Reasoning.

papers.title: InversionView: A General-Purpose Method for Reading Information from Neural Activations
papers.research_question: How can we decipher the information encoded in neural activations? The paper proposes InversionView, a method to sample from the preimage of an activation to uncover the information content.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces InversionView, a method that samples from the preimage of an activation via a conditional decoder to uncover the information encoded in neural activations and understand model algorithms.
papers.conclusion: InversionView is a general-purpose method that effectively deciphers information in neural activations, enabling better understanding of model algorithms and simplifying interpretability workflows.
papers.key_findings:
InversionView can reveal both basic and complex information in activations, such as token counts and relative positions.
InversionView simplifies interpretability workflows, agreeing with prior circuit findings in GPT-2 small.
InversionView enabled the first fully verified circuit for a 3-digit addition model.
InversionView scales to larger models like GPT-2 for factual recall.
papers.limitation:
Training a decoder requires a dataset of activations and can be computationally expensive.
The decoder may not perfectly capture the preimage, leading to potential biases in the generated samples.
The method is currently limited to discrete sequences (text).
future_direction: Extend InversionView to continuous domains.
Improve decoder efficiency.
Automate interpretation using LLMs.
papers.abstract: The inner workings of neural networks can be better understood if we can fully decipher the information encoded in neural activations. In this paper, we argue that this information is embodied by the subset of inputs that give rise to similar activations. We propose InversionView, which allows us to practically inspect this subset by sampling from a trained decoder model conditioned on activations. This helps uncover the information content of activation vectors, and facilitates understanding of the algorithms implemented by transformer models. We present four case studies where we investigate models ranging from small transformers to GPT-2. In these studies, we show that InversionView can reveal clear information contained in activations, including basic information about tokens appearing in the context, as well as more complex information, such as the count of certain tokens, their relative positions, and abstract knowledge about the subject. We also provide causally verified circuits to confirm the decoded information.

papers.title: Tracing the Roots of Facts in Multilingual Language Models: Independent, Shared, and Transferred Knowledge
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how multilingual language models acquire and represent factual knowledge across languages, specifically examining the factors affecting probing performance, whether fact representations are shared or independent across languages, and how cross-lingual representations are formed.
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes methods for distinguishing three types of fact representations in multilingual language models (language-independent, cross-lingual shared, and cross-lingual transferred) and reveals the challenges in cross-lingual factual knowledge transfer.
papers.conclusion: Our research establishes the groundwork for further studies in understanding cross-lingual factual knowledge representation and highlights the challenges in achieving effective cross-lingual transfer of factual knowledge from high-resource to low-resource languages in ML-LMs.
papers.key_findings:
Factual probing performance across languages shows moderate correlation with training data volume and strong negative correlation with mask token count.
There are localized knowledge sharing patterns among geographically proximate languages.
ML-LMs exhibit both language-independent and cross-lingual fact representations, even for the same fact.
Active fact neurons in low-resource languages are more active and distributed in shallow layers compared to high-resource languages.
Cross-lingual transfer of factual knowledge does occur but is limited, and many correctly predicted facts in low-resource languages can be attributed to simple inference patterns rather than true transfer.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to encoder-based models (mBERT and XLM-R) and may not generalize to large decoder-based multilingual models.
future_direction: Enhance the cross-lingual fact representation learning in ML-LMs.
Develop a more precise factual probing dataset.
papers.abstract: Acquiring factual knowledge for language models (LMs) in low-resource languages poses a serious challenge, thus resorting to cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LMs (ML-LMs).In this study, we ask how ML-LMs acquire and represent factual knowledge.Using the multilingual factual knowledge probing dataset, mLAMA, we first conducted a neuron investigation of ML-LMs (specifically, multilingual BERT).We then traced the roots of facts back to the knowledge source (Wikipedia) to identify the ways in which ML-LMs acquire specific facts.We finally identified three patterns of acquiring and representing facts in ML-LMs: languageindependent, cross-lingual shared and transferred, and devised methods for differentiating them.Our findings highlight the challenge of maintaining consistent factual knowledge across languages, underscoring the need for better fact representation learning in ML-LMs. 1

papers.title: Placing language in an integrated understanding system: Next steps toward human-level performance in neural language models
papers.research_question: What is the role of language in human intelligence and how can we extend current machine language models to achieve human-level language understanding by integrating language with other modalities and memory systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a framework for building an integrated understanding system that combines insights from cognitive neuroscience and artificial intelligence, using query-based attention and memory systems to extend current language models toward human-level language understanding.
papers.conclusion: Combining insights from neuroscience and AI will take us closer to human-level language understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Current language models are limited by their focus on language-internal tasks and lack of memory for remote information.
The human brain integrates language with other modalities and uses complementary learning systems (neocortex and medial temporal lobe) for understanding.
Query-based attention is a key innovation that can be extended to integrate multiple modalities and memory.
Future models should incorporate an MTL-like memory to handle remote information and improve data efficiency.
Understanding should be seen as constructing situation representations, which are compositional and grounded in multi-sensory experience.
papers.limitation: The proposed sketch leaves important issues open and will require substantial development.
future_direction: Incorporating an MTL-like memory to allow the use of remote information beyond the current episode.
Integrating a frontal lobe-like subsystem to guide processing according to task demands.
Extending the approach beyond concrete situations to abstract ones involving laws, belief systems, and scientific theories.
papers.abstract: Language is crucial for human intelligence, but what exactly is its role? We take language to be a part of a system for understanding and communicating about situations. In humans, these abilities emerge gradually from experience and depend on domain-general principles of biological neural networks: connection-based learning, distributed representation, and context-sensitive, mutual constraint satisfaction-based processing. Current artificial language processing systems rely on the same domain general principles, embodied in artificial neural networks. Indeed, recent progress in this field depends on query-based attention, which extends the ability of these systems to exploit context and has contributed to remarkable breakthroughs. Nevertheless, most current models focus exclusively on language-internal tasks, limiting their ability to perform tasks that depend on understanding situations. These systems also lack memory for the contents of prior situations outside of a fixed contextual span. We describe the organization of the brain's distributed understanding system, which includes a fast learning system that addresses the memory problem. We sketch a framework for future models of understanding drawing equally on cognitive neuroscience and artificial intelligence and exploiting query-based attention. We highlight relevant current directions and consider further developments needed to fully capture human-level language understanding in a computational system.

papers.title: Mass-Editing Memory with Attention in Transformers: A cross-lingual exploration of knowledge
papers.research_question: This study examines the effectiveness of existing knowledge editing methods across languages and investigates the role of attention mechanisms in this process.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes MEMAT, a knowledge editing method that modifies attention heads in addition to MLP layers, leading to improved performance, cross-lingual portability, and enhanced model understanding of edited facts.
papers.conclusion: MEMAT improves knowledge editing by leveraging attention heads, demonstrating portability and effectiveness across languages, and enhancing the model's understanding of the inserted factual associations.
papers.key_findings:
MEMIT's cross-lingual performance is dependent on subject tokenization similarity between languages.
Attention heads encode language-independent information about factual associations, achieving high accuracy in classifying truthful sentences.
MEMAT outperforms MEMIT across all evaluation metrics (success and magnitude), with improvements exceeding 10% in some cases.
The attention head corrections learned by MEMAT are portable and can be recycled for editing new sets of factual triplets.
MEMAT enhances the model's comprehension of the edited knowledge rather than merely reintroducing it, as evidenced by improved paraphrase and neighborhood metrics.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to English and Catalan; generalization to other linguistic contexts may be limited due to alphabet similarity.
Broader challenges in knowledge editing persist, such as the inability to modify related knowledge and lack of bidirectionality.
future_direction: Investigating language adaptation techniques to enable models to perform tasks in a more language-agnostic manner.
Exploring the role that each architecture component plays in alternative domains to enhance explainable AI.
papers.abstract: Recent research has explored methods for updating and modifying factual knowledge in large language models, often focusing on specific multi-layer perceptron blocks. This study expands on this work by examining the effectiveness of existing knowledge editing methods across languages and delving into the role of attention mechanisms in this process. Drawing from the insights gained, we propose Mass-Editing Memory with Attention in Transformers (MEMAT), a method that achieves significant improvements in all metrics while requiring minimal parameter modifications. MEMAT delivers a remarkable 10% increase in magnitude metrics, benefits languages not included in the training data and also demonstrates a high degree of portability. Our code and data are at https://github.com/dtamayo-nlp/MEMAT.

papers.title: Plausibility Processing in Transformer Language Models: Focusing on the Role of Attention Heads in GPT
papers.research_question: How do Transformer language models process semantic knowledge, specifically the plausibility of noun-verb relations, and what is the causal role of attention heads in this processing?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that GPT2 processes noun-verb plausibility similarly to humans and identifies a set of attention heads that detect plausibility. It shows these heads collectively and causally contribute to the model's plausibility processing, with contributions being imbalanced and not strictly correlated with individual head performance.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that semantic plausibility knowledge in GPT2 is processed by a diffusely distributed set of attention heads that make imbalanced but collective causal contributions, highlighting the importance of causal analysis in understanding attention head functions.
papers.key_findings:
GPT2 exhibits a higher degree of similarity with humans in plausibility processing compared to other Transformer models (BERT, RoBERTa, ALBERT).
GPT2 contains 18 attention heads distributed across layers that are sensitive to noun-verb plausibility, independent of syntactic dependency.
Pruning these plausibility-processing heads eliminates GPT2's plausibility sensitivity, while pruning a random set of heads does not.
The causal contribution of individual plausibility-processing heads to the model's overall ability is imbalanced; a single head (0,10) accounts for a large portion of the effect for syntactic dependents.
The performance of an attention head in detecting plausibility (accuracy) does not necessarily correlate with its causal contribution to the model's overall plausibility processing ability.
papers.limitation:
The scope of the study is restricted to the plausibility of noun-verb relations, not covering other types of semantic knowledge.
The study does not detail how attention heads interact with other components like hidden states across layers or feed-forward networks.
future_direction: Expand the study's scope to a broader array of semantic knowledge for better generalizability.
Investigate interactions between attention heads and other model components (e.g., hidden states, feed-forward networks) to better understand their role in semantic knowledge processing.
papers.abstract: The goal of this paper is to explore how Transformer language models process semantic knowledge, especially regarding the plausibility of noun-verb relations. First, I demonstrate GPT2 exhibits a higher degree of similarity with humans in plausibility processing compared to other Transformer language models. Next, I delve into how knowledge of plausibility is contained within attention heads of GPT2 and how these heads causally contribute to GPT2's plausibility processing ability. Through several experiments, it was found that: i) GPT2 has a number of attention heads that detect plausible noun-verb relationships; ii) these heads collectively contribute to the Transformer's ability to process plausibility, albeit to varying degrees; and iii) attention heads' individual performance in detecting plausibility does not necessarily correlate with how much they contribute to GPT2's plausibility processing ability.

papers.title: Uncovering Intermediate Variables in Transformers using Circuit Probing
papers.research_question: How can we automatically uncover low-level circuits that compute hypothesized intermediate variables in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit probing, a method that combines probing and causal analysis to automatically uncover circuits computing hypothesized intermediate variables in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Circuit probing provides a unified approach for a variety of analyses, combining and extending the capabilities of existing methods for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit probing can decipher the algorithms learned by models on simple arithmetic tasks.
Circuit probing reveals modular structure within a model, showing that shared and free variables are computed by distinct circuits.
Circuit probing tracks the development of circuits over training, showing circuit formation occurs continuously before generalization.
Circuit probing uncovers circuits responsible for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora in GPT2-Small and Medium.
Circuit probing is more faithful to the underlying model computation than linear probing, nonlinear probing, and amnesic probing.
papers.limitation: Neurons are typically polysemantic, so the assumption that a circuit is only causally implicated in computing a single intermediate variable may not hold completely.
papers.abstract: Neural network models have achieved high performance on a wide variety of complex tasks, but the algorithms that they implement are notoriously difficult to interpret. It is often necessary to hypothesize intermediate variables involved in a network's computation in order to understand these algorithms. For example, does a language model depend on particular syntactic properties when generating a sentence? Yet, existing analysis tools make it difficult to test hypotheses of this type. We propose a new analysis technique - circuit probing - that automatically uncovers low-level circuits that compute hypothesized intermediate variables. This enables causal analysis through targeted ablation at the level of model parameters. We apply this method to models trained on simple arithmetic tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness at (1) deciphering the algorithms that models have learned, (2) revealing modular structure within a model, and (3) tracking the development of circuits over training. Across these three experiments we demonstrate that circuit probing combines and extends the capabilities of existing methods, providing one unified approach for a variety of analyses. Finally, we demonstrate circuit probing on a real-world use case: uncovering circuits that are responsible for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora in GPT2-Small and Medium.

papers.title: Co-occurrence is not Factual Association in Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do language models struggle to learn novel factual knowledge effectively from finetuning on limited textual demonstrations? Is it because they learn word co-occurrence statistics instead of true factual associations?
papers.core_contribution: Language models are biased to learn word co-occurrence statistics instead of true factual associations. We propose two strategies to improve learning of factual associations: using text with implicit associations and active forgetting.
papers.conclusion: Language models are biased to learn co-occurrence statistics, which hinders learning of generalizable factual knowledge. Using implicit association text and active forgetting can improve learning of factual associations.
papers.key_findings:
Co-occurrence statistics are easily learned from text with explicit co-occurrence, while factual associations are more easily learned from text with implicit association.
Knowledge in the form of co-occurrence statistics does not generalize well beyond simple QA, while factual associations generalize well to reasoning tasks.
Co-occurrence statistics and factual associations are parameterized in different layers: co-occurrence in middle layers, factual associations in lower layers.
Training on text with implicit association improves generalization of learned knowledge.
Active forgetting (resetting upper layer parameters) unblocks learning of factual associations and improves generalization.
papers.limitation:
Variation in forms of text: only two forms of text expressing factual knowledge are considered.
Methods for text generation: turning general text into text with implicit association may require complex rewriting.
The study is limited to finetuning of pretrained models, not pretraining from scratch.
Relationship to knowledge editing, knowledge-aware training and assisted reasoning: the study focuses on learning from raw text without annotations or reasoning assistance.
future_direction: Expand the investigation of knowledge learning efficiency to the pretraining phase.
Explore scalable data generation methods for efficient knowledge learning.
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models can encode a large amount of knowledge and utilize it for various reasoning tasks, yet they can still struggle to learn novel factual knowledge effectively from finetuning on limited textual demonstrations. In this work, we show that the reason for this deficiency is that language models are biased to learn word co-occurrence statistics instead of true factual associations. We identify the differences between two forms of knowledge representation in language models: knowledge in the form of co-occurrence statistics is encoded in the middle layers of the transformer model and does not generalize well to reasoning scenarios beyond simple question answering, while true factual associations are encoded in the lower layers and can be freely utilized in various reasoning tasks. Based on these observations, we propose two strategies to improve the learning of factual associations in language models. We show that training on text with implicit rather than explicit factual associations can force the model to learn factual associations instead of co-occurrence statistics, significantly improving the generalization of newly learned knowledge. We also propose a simple training method to actively forget the learned co-occurrence statistics, which unblocks and enhances the learning of factual associations when training on plain narrative text. On both synthetic and real-world corpora, the two proposed strategies improve the generalization of the knowledge learned during finetuning to reasoning scenarios such as indirect and multi-hop question answering.

papers.title: Promote, Suppress, Iterate: How Language Models Answer One-to-Many Factual Queries
papers.research_question: How do language models internally implement and integrate knowledge recall and repetition avoidance for one-to-many factual queries?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a promote-then-suppress mechanism in language models for one-to-many factual queries, where attention propagates subject information and MLPs promote answers, then attention suppresses previous answers with MLPs amplifying the suppression signal.
papers.conclusion: LMs promote all answers and then suppress previously generated ones, using attention and MLPs to integrate subject and previous answer tokens for knowledge recall and repetition avoidance.
papers.key_findings:
LMs first promote all possible answers and then suppress previously generated ones.
Attention copies subject information to the last token, and MLPs use this information to promote answers.
Previous answer tokens are used for both knowledge recall (promoting new answers) and suppression.
Attention suppresses previous answers, and MLPs amplify this suppression signal.
The last token aggregates knowledge recall and suppression information to generate distinct answers.
papers.limitation:
Low accuracy due to long-tail entities, outdated datasets, and strict exact-match evaluation.
Analysis focuses only on correct cases, not on errors or unreliable signals.
future_direction: Investigate possible redundancies in how LMs encode knowledge across multiple tokens.
Examine patterns when LMs use unreliable signals or make errors.
papers.abstract: To answer one-to-many factual queries (e.g., listing cities of a country), a language model (LM) must simultaneously recall knowledge and avoid repeating previous answers. How are these two subtasks implemented and integrated internally? Across multiple datasets, models, and prompt templates, we identify a promote-then-suppress mechanism: the model first recalls all answers, and then suppresses previously generated ones. Specifically, LMs use both the subject and previous answer tokens to perform knowledge recall, with attention propagating subject information and MLPs promoting the answers. Then, attention attends to and suppresses previous answer tokens, while MLPs amplify the suppression signal. Our mechanism is corroborated by extensive experimental evidence: in addition to using early decoding and causal tracing, we analyze how components use different tokens by introducing both Token Lens, which decodes aggregated attention updates from specified tokens, and a knockout method that analyzes changes in MLP outputs after removing attention to specified tokens. Overall, we provide new insights into how LMs' internal components interact with different input tokens to support complex factual recall. Code is available at https://github.com/Lorenayannnnn/how-lms-answer-one-to-many-factual-queries.

papers.title: Language Model Circuits Are Sparse in the Neuron Basis
papers.research_question: Can MLP neurons serve as a sparse basis for circuit tracing, comparable to sparse autoencoders (SAEs)?
papers.core_contribution: MLP neurons are as sparse a feature basis as SAEs for circuit tracing, enabling effective circuit tracing without additional training costs.
papers.conclusion: MLP neurons provide a sparse basis for circuit tracing, advancing automated interpretability without additional training.
papers.key_findings:
MLP activations are a much sparser basis than MLP outputs for circuit tracing, reducing circuit size by 100x.
Using RelP attribution closes the performance gap between MLP activations and SAE features.
The findings hold even with unpaired data (without counterfactual inputs).
RelP finds more faithful edges than Integrated Gradients for circuit tracing.
In a multi-hop reasoning task, small sets of neurons encode specific latent reasoning steps and can be steered to change model output.
papers.abstract: The high-level concepts that a neural network uses to perform computation need not be aligned to individual neurons (Smolensky, 1986). Language model interpretability research has thus turned to techniques such as \textit{sparse autoencoders} (SAEs) to decompose the neuron basis into more interpretable units of model computation, for tasks such as \textit{circuit tracing}. However, not all neuron-based representations are uninterpretable. For the first time, we empirically show that \textbf{MLP neurons are as sparse a feature basis as SAEs}. We use this finding to develop an end-to-end pipeline for circuit tracing on the MLP neuron basis, which locates causal circuitry on a variety of tasks using gradient-based attribution. On a standard subject-verb agreement benchmark (Marks et al., 2025), a circuit of $\approx 10^2$ MLP neurons is enough to control model behaviour. On the multi-hop city $\to$ state $\to$ capital task from Lindsey et al., 2025, we find a circuit in which small sets of neurons encode specific latent reasoning steps (e.g.~`map city to its state'), and can be steered to change the model's output. This work thus advances automated interpretability of language models without additional training costs.

papers.title: Mechanistic Indicators of Understanding in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) possess genuine understanding, and if so, what forms does it take? The paper investigates this by synthesizing findings from mechanistic interpretability within a philosophical framework.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a tiered framework (conceptual, state-of-the-world, principled understanding) for assessing understanding in LLMs and synthesizes mechanistic interpretability evidence to argue that LLMs can develop internal organizations that underwrite understanding-like unification, though these mechanisms diverge from human cognition.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability reveals internal organizations in LLMs that can underwrite understanding-like unification across conceptual, factual, and principled tiers, but these mechanisms diverge from human cognition in their parallel exploitation of heterogeneous, task-specific pathways.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs develop internal 'features' (e.g., a 'Golden Gate Bridge' feature in Claude 3 Sonnet) that act as conceptual unifiers, connecting diverse manifestations of entities or properties.
The linear representation hypothesis is supported, with features encoded as directions in latent space, and superposition allows for efficient representation of many features.
Models like Othello-GPT develop internal 'world models' (e.g., of the board state) that are causally involved in task performance, as shown via probing and intervention techniques.
The phenomenon of 'grokking' demonstrates a shift from memorization to discovering compact, generalizable circuits (e.g., for modular arithmetic), indicative of principled understanding.
Higher-tier understanding mechanisms coexist with lower-tier heuristics (e.g., memorization, n-gram statistics) within LLMs, impacting their epistemic trustworthiness.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often portrayed as merely imitating linguistic patterns without genuine understanding. We argue that recent findings in mechanistic interpretability (MI), the emerging field probing the inner workings of LLMs, render this picture increasingly untenable--but only once those findings are integrated within a theoretical account of understanding. We propose a tiered framework for thinking about understanding in LLMs and use it to synthesize the most relevant findings to date. The framework distinguishes three hierarchical varieties of understanding, each tied to a corresponding level of computational organization: conceptual understanding emerges when a model forms "features" as directions in latent space, learning connections between diverse manifestations of a single entity or property; state-of-the-world understanding emerges when a model learns contingent factual connections between features and dynamically tracks changes in the world; principled understanding emerges when a model ceases to rely on memorized facts and discovers a compact "circuit" connecting these facts. Across these tiers, MI uncovers internal organizations that can underwrite understanding-like unification. However, these also diverge from human cognition in their parallel exploitation of heterogeneous mechanisms. Fusing philosophical theory with mechanistic evidence thus allows us to transcend binary debates over whether AI understands, paving the way for a comparative, mechanistically grounded epistemology that explores how AI understanding aligns with--and diverges from--our own.

papers.title: Scaling sparse feature circuit finding for in-context learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to understand the mechanism of in-context learning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify task-detection and task-execution features in the in-context learning circuit of large language models, and introduces the Task Vector Cleaning algorithm to decompose task vectors into interpretable features.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance understanding of in-context learning mechanisms and demonstrate the potential of sparse autoencoders as a powerful tool for interpretability research on larger language models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can be used to analyze in-context learning in larger models like Gemma-1 2B, scaling up circuit analysis.
Task-execution features encode task knowledge and can causally induce task zero-shot performance.
Task-detection features identify tasks from the prompt and are causally linked to execution features via attention and MLP sublayers.
The Task Vector Cleaning algorithm effectively decomposes task vectors into sparse, interpretable features while preserving their effect on loss.
The in-context learning circuit involves interaction between detection and execution features through attention and MLP layers.
papers.limitation:
Circuit search was constrained to intermediate layers due to early layers processing token-level information and having lower quality Indirect Effect approximations.
Hundreds of features needed to be ablated to achieve significant faithfulness degradation, unlike prior work which required fewer.
Negative steering experiments showed lower task specificity, indicating steering experiments alone may not suffice for comprehensive analysis.
future_direction: Improving SAE training to yield more monosemantic features.
Scaling circuit analysis to even larger models.
Applying these techniques to more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular tool for interpreting large language model activations, but their utility in addressing open questions in interpretability remains unclear. In this work, we demonstrate their effectiveness by using SAEs to deepen our understanding of the mechanism behind in-context learning (ICL). We identify abstract SAE features that (i) encode the model's knowledge of which task to execute and (ii) whose latent vectors causally induce the task zero-shot. This aligns with prior work showing that ICL is mediated by task vectors. We further demonstrate that these task vectors are well approximated by a sparse sum of SAE latents, including these task-execution features. To explore the ICL mechanism, we adapt the sparse feature circuits methodology of Marks et al. (2024) to work for the much larger Gemma-1 2B model, with 30 times as many parameters, and to the more complex task of ICL. Through circuit finding, we discover task-detecting features with corresponding SAE latents that activate earlier in the prompt, that detect when tasks have been performed. They are causally linked with task-execution features through the attention and MLP sublayers.

papers.title: Latent Concept Disentanglement in Transformer-based Language Models
papers.research_question: How do transformers represent latent structures when performing in-context learning? Do they disentangle and compose latent concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that transformers disentangle and compose latent concepts during in-context learning, representing them in low-dimensional subspaces that reflect the geometry of the latent parameters.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are capable of disentangling and composing latent concepts during in-context learning, with internal representations that capture the geometry of the underlying latent parameters.
papers.key_findings:
For multi-hop reasoning tasks, the model uses step-by-step composition of latent concepts via a sparse set of attention heads.
The bridge-resolving mechanism is much stronger in the larger 27B model compared to the 2B model, indicating model size benefits latent concept disentanglement.
Adding more in-context examples strengthens the causal importance of the relevant sub-circuits and increases concept representation disentanglement.
For numerical tasks with latent parameters, task vectors lie on low-dimensional smooth manifolds that reflect the geometry of the underlying parameter (e.g., radius).
Interpolating along the task vector manifold allows steering the model's computation, approximately interpolating the latent parameter.
papers.limitation:
Only English language queries are used, so mechanisms may differ across languages.
The latent concepts tested are all human-interpretable (e.g., numbers, countries), limiting generalization to more intricate relationships.
papers.abstract: When large language models (LLMs) use in-context learning (ICL) to solve a new task, they must infer latent concepts from demonstration examples. This raises the question of whether and how transformers represent latent structures as part of their computation. Our work experiments with several controlled tasks, studying this question using mechanistic interpretability. First, we show that in transitive reasoning tasks with a latent, discrete concept, the model successfully identifies the latent concept and does step-by-step concept composition. This builds upon prior work that analyzes single-step reasoning. Then, we consider tasks parameterized by a latent numerical concept. We discover low-dimensional subspaces in the model's representation space, where the geometry cleanly reflects the underlying parameterization. Overall, we show that small and large models can indeed disentangle and utilize latent concepts that they learn in-context from a handful of abbreviated demonstrations.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in Mamba
papers.research_question: Does factual recall in the Mamba state space model exhibit locality similar to the patterns observed in autoregressive transformer language models?
papers.core_contribution: Despite architectural differences, Mamba exhibits similar localization patterns for factual recall as transformers, and many interpretability methods developed for transformers can be adapted to Mamba.
papers.conclusion: Many interpretability methods from transformers can be adapted to Mamba, and factual recall in Mamba shows similar localization patterns, indicating architectural similarities in how different models store and recall facts.
papers.key_findings:
Activation patching in Mamba reveals high causal effects at early-middle layers (subject last token) and later layers (prompt last token), similar to transformers.
ROME editing can successfully insert facts in Mamba by modifying projection matrices, with Wo being the most effective.
The linearity of relation decoding (LRE) in Mamba is similar to transformers, with some relations being more linearly decodable than others.
Adapted attention knockout experiments show that Mamba propagates relation information in early layers and subject information in middle layers, similar to information flow in transformers.
There is a separation of roles between early-mid and later layers in Mamba for factual recall, analogous to findings in transformers.
papers.limitation: Performing attention knockout in Mamba is challenging due to the Conv+SSM operation, making it difficult to block specific edges like in transformers.
papers.abstract: We investigate the mechanisms of factual recall in the Mamba state space model. Our work is inspired by previous findings in autoregressive transformer language models suggesting that their knowledge recall is localized to particular modules at specific token locations; we therefore ask whether factual recall in Mamba can be similarly localized. To investigate this, we conduct four lines of experiments on Mamba. First, we apply causal tracing or interchange interventions to localize key components inside Mamba that are responsible for recalling facts, revealing that specific components within middle layers show strong causal effects at the last token of the subject, while the causal effect of intervening on later layers is most pronounced at the last token of the prompt, matching previous findings on autoregressive transformers. Second, we show that rank-one model editing methods can successfully insert facts at specific locations, again resembling findings on transformer LMs. Third, we examine the linearity of Mamba's representations of factual relations. Finally we adapt attention-knockout techniques to Mamba in order to dissect information flow during factual recall. We compare Mamba directly to a similar-sized autoregressive transformer LM and conclude that despite significant differences in architectural approach, when it comes to factual recall, the two architectures share many similarities.

papers.title: A Modular Dataset to Demonstrate LLM Abstraction Capability
papers.research_question: Do LLMs have an internal representation of reasoning correctness and abstraction in reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally encode representations of reasoning correctness, with strongest signals in middle-late layers, and they distinguish between logical and semantic equivalence in abstract reasoning concepts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess internal representations of reasoning correctness and abstraction, which can inform future efforts to enhance model reliability, interpretability, and trustworthiness.
papers.key_findings:
A classifier trained on LLM activations achieves over 80% accuracy in predicting reasoning step correctness.
LLMs have internal representations of reasoning correctness, strongest in middle-late Transformer layers.
LLMs encode abstract reasoning concepts that separate logical from semantic equivalence.
Abstraction level varies across layers, with middle layers containing more abstract information.
The reasoning representations are similar across top-performing layers, suggesting redundant encoding.
papers.limitation:
Analysis restricted to structured logic puzzles, may not generalize to real-world scenarios.
Classifier's success may not generalize to other types of reasoning problems.
Reliance on probing techniques does not provide mechanistic explanation of how representations emerge.
Classifier trained on single LLM architecture, generalizability across models unclear.
future_direction: Explore more diverse reasoning benchmarks.
Conduct broader cross-model analyses including LRM models.
Develop methods for directly steering LLM reasoning based on learned representations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive capabilities but struggle with reasoning errors due to hallucinations and flawed logic. To investigate their internal representations of reasoning, we introduce ArrangementPuzzle, a novel puzzle dataset with structured solutions and automated stepwise correctness verification. We trained a classifier model on LLM activations on this dataset and found that it achieved over 80% accuracy in predicting reasoning correctness, implying that LLMs internally distinguish between correct and incorrect reasoning steps, with the strongest representations in middle-late Transformer layers. Further analysis reveals that LLMs encode abstract reasoning concepts within the middle activation layers of the transformer architecture, distinguishing logical from semantic equivalence. These findings provide insights into LLM reasoning mechanisms and contribute to improving AI reliability and interpretability, thereby offering the possibility to manipulate and refine LLM reasoning.

papers.title: An Investigation of Neuron Activation as a Unified Lens to Explain Chain-of-Thought Eliciting Arithmetic Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: How can neuron activation in feed-forward layers of LLMs provide a unified explanation for the importance of various components in Chain-of-Thought prompts for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that analyzing the activation of reasoning neurons in feed-forward layers provides a unified explanation for why certain components (e.g., equations, textual explanation) in Chain-of-Thought prompts are important for eliciting arithmetic reasoning in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Neuron activation analysis provides valuable insights into the internal mechanism of LLMs for arithmetic reasoning and can explain prior empirical observations about Chain-of-Thought prompting.
papers.key_findings:
The paper discovered 113 neurons in Llama2-7B associated with arithmetic reasoning concepts such as logical connectors and arithmetic operations.
Corrupting the discovered reasoning neurons via random noise ablation leads to a significant performance drop, demonstrating their importance for eliciting reasoning.
The presence of equations and textual explanation in CoT prompts leads to higher activation of reasoning neurons, explaining their importance for performance.
Diversity of arithmetic operators in prompts leads to activation of a broader set of reasoning neurons, which improves model performance.
Incorrect in-distribution labels do not substantially affect reasoning neuron activation, while out-of-distribution labels cause different activation patterns and lower performance.
papers.limitation:
Neuron activation is necessary but not sufficient to completely explain LLM reasoning; interactions among components are also important.
The seven pre-defined concepts used may not cover the full scope of arithmetic reasoning, and activation can be faked by prompting.
Analysis was performed primarily on Llama2-7B; generalization to other LLMs may require different approaches.
future_direction: Future work should combine neuron activation analysis with other approaches like circuit analysis and top-down methods for a more complete understanding.
Extend the research to other LLMs and more comprehensive sets of reasoning concepts.
Systematically explore the potential of predicting LLM reasoning performance via neuron activation without human labels.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong arithmetic reasoning capabilities when prompted with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompts. However, we have only a limited understanding of how they are processed by LLMs. To demystify it, prior work has primarily focused on ablating different components in the CoT prompt and empirically observing their resulting LLM performance change. Yet, the reason why these components are important to LLM reasoning is not explored. To fill this gap, in this work, we investigate ``neuron activation'' as a lens to provide a unified explanation to observations made by prior work. Specifically, we look into neurons within the feed-forward layers of LLMs that may have activated their arithmetic reasoning capabilities, using Llama2 as an example. To facilitate this investigation, we also propose an approach based on GPT-4 to automatically identify neurons that imply arithmetic reasoning. Our analyses revealed that the activation of reasoning neurons in the feed-forward layers of an LLM can explain the importance of various components in a CoT prompt, and future research can extend it for a more complete understanding.

papers.title: Making sense of transformer success
papers.research_question: How do the relatively simple algorithmic components of neural language models (NLMs) provide them with genuine linguistic competence and the ability to think?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides an epistemological analysis of existing explanatory strategies for transformer-based neural language models, arguing they are analogous to those used in cognitive science to explain human intelligence.
papers.conclusion: The explanatory strategies advanced to explain NLMs do not differ from those used in the philosophy of mind to explain natural cognitive systems, but the explanatory gap for NLMs challenges the simulative method in cognitive science.
papers.key_findings:
The central philosophical question in AI has shifted from 'can machines think?' to 'how can machines think?', pointing to an explanatory gap for NLMs.
Existing explanatory strategies for NLMs (functional, mechanistic, simulative) do not differ from those used in cognitive science to explain human intelligent behaviors.
The 'copying algorithm' and 'induction head' phenomena in a Transformer provide a mechanistic explanation of in-context learning.
Current attempts to use NLMs to predict brain activation patterns involve a 'co-simulation', where the NLM and the brain are used to simulate and understand each other.
The explanatory gap for NLMs challenges the simulative method in cognitive science, which uses artificial systems to understand the mind.
papers.abstract: This article provides an epistemological analysis of current attempts of explaining how the relatively simple algorithmic components of neural language models (NLMs) provide them with genuine linguistic competence. After introducing the Transformer architecture, at the basis of most of current NLMs, the paper firstly emphasizes how the central question in the philosophy of AI has been shifted from "can machines think?", as originally put by Alan Turing, to "how can machines think?", pointing to an explanatory gap for NLMs. Subsequently, existing explanatory strategies for the functioning of NLMs are analyzed to argue that they, however debated, do not differ from the explanatory strategies used in cognitive science to explain intelligent behaviors of humans. In particular, available experimental studies turned to test the theory of mind, discourse entity tracking, and property induction in NLMs are examined under the light of the functional analysis in the philosophy of cognitive science; the so-called copying algorithm and the induction head phenomenon of a Transformer are shown to provide a mechanist explanation of in-context learning; finally, current pioneering attempts to use NLMs to predict brain activation patterns when processing language are here shown to involve what we call a co-simulation, in which a NLM and the brain are used to simulate and understand each other.

papers.title: The Queen of England is not England's Queen: On the Lack of Factual Coherency in PLMs
papers.research_question: What is the coherency of factual knowledge in Pre-trained Language Models, and how does it vary with different prompts and evidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the concept of coherency for factual knowledge in PLMs, demonstrates that PLMs have low coherency, and finds that including evidence paragraphs substantially improves coherency.
papers.conclusion: PLMs have poor coherency in factual knowledge, but evidence paragraphs help. Future work should focus on architectural, data, and interface improvements.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs have low coherency in factual knowledge.
Autoregressive PLMs perform worse than masked PLMs.
Optimized prompts do not improve coherency.
Including evidence paragraphs substantially improves coherency.
Coherency varies significantly with paraphrased prompts.
papers.limitation: For N-1 or N-M relations, it is difficult to exclude every possible answer, and only answers present in LAMA are excluded, which might negatively affect the results.
future_direction: Improve PLMs on architectural level.
Improve PLMs on data level.
Improve pre-training objectives and interface.
papers.abstract: Factual knowledge encoded in Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) enriches their representations and justifies their use as knowledge bases. Previous work has focused on probing PLMs for factual knowledge by measuring how often they can correctly predict an object entity given a subject and a relation, and improving fact retrieval by optimizing the prompts used for querying PLMs. In this work, we consider a complementary aspect, namely the coherency of factual knowledge in PLMs, i.e., how often can PLMs predict the subject entity given its initial prediction of the object entity. This goes beyond evaluating how much PLMs know, and focuses on the internal state of knowledge inside them. Our results indicate that PLMs have low coherency using manually written, optimized and paraphrased prompts, but including an evidence paragraph leads to substantial improvement. This shows that PLMs fail to model inverse relations and need further enhancements to be able to handle retrieving facts from their parameters in a coherent manner, and to be considered as knowledge bases.

papers.title: Conceptual structure coheres in human cognition but not in large language models
papers.research_question: Does conceptual structure in large language models cohere across different probing tasks as it does in humans, or do human and LLM conceptual representations differ in robustness?
papers.core_contribution: Human conceptual structure is robust across different tasks and cultures, but large language models exhibit less coherence in conceptual structure across different probing tasks, indicating a lack of a stable conceptual core.
